det.desc: This is the "Art Print Version" of the Hero Complex Gallery release of the Back to the Future one sheet print, (which omits the movie title and billing block text) from a strictly limited timed run of 527 prints plus Artist Proofs, hand-numbered in the bottom right margin 59/527. Produced as an 18-color screen print measuring 24" x 36" on archival paper with a white border. It was created directly from scans of Struzan's original 1985 painting and color-approved by the artist. Hand-signed by Drew Struzan in silver/white ink in the lower-left corner. During the original Hero Complex Gallery timed release, the print retailed for $135, with an optional $50 add-on for Struzan's signature. Including the Certificate of Authenticity which confirms this specific signature was witnessed by HCG on March 9, 2018, in Pasadena, CA. The beloved artist Drew Struzan, passed away on 10/13/2025, making this piece highly collectible, as the artist stopped signing around 2020, due to Alzheimer’s disease. There is a small crease on the top left corner. Which should not be visible and will flatten when framed. Sold as is, no returns.

Silversmiths in Newburyport, Massachusetts, often crafted decorative serving pieces like this to bring traditional elegance into everyday middle-class homes. They were made during the mid-20th century to serve sweets, nuts, or small candies during formal gatherings and family celebrations. Craftsmen created these pieces by stamping base metal alloys with heavy hydraulic presses before applying a fine layer of silver plate and detailed hand-buffing. Middle-class families used them on coffee tables, sideboards, and dining tables during holidays and special visits. Over time, as formal entertaining declined and modern stainless steel became popular for daily use, these decorative silver-plated dishes transitioned from dining tables to enclosed display cabinets.

det.desc: Classical devotional imagery meets surreal distortion in this large original acrylic painting on canvas. A nursing child, encircled by a gold-toned halo, looks directly toward the viewer against a softly colored field of blush pink, ivory and pale yellow. Cascading, milk-like forms introduce a dreamlike quality, balancing maternal tenderness with an unsettling visual tension. The composition invites comparison with Madonna and Child imagery, particularly the tradition of the nursing Madonna. Read symbolically, the descending white forms suggest nourishment from a divine source, while the child’s unusually knowing gaze lends the figure a sense of spiritual awareness. These are interpretive possibilities rather than documented statements of the artist’s intent. Smoothly blended flesh tones and carefully modeled features contrast with the exaggerated drips surrounding them. That interplay allows a satirical reading: the painting adopts the visual authority of classical religious art while playfully disrupting its composure.
